name: Vithoba
role: Beloved deity of Pandharpur and the Varkari pilgrims
summary: Vithoba, also called Vitthal, is worshipped in Pandharpur in Maharashtra, usually as a form of Vishnu or Krishna. Varkari saints sing of him, and pilgrims walk for days to see him.
about: Vithoba, also known as Vitthala or Panduranga, is the main deity of Pandharpur on the Bhima river in Maharashtra. Most devotees see him as a form of Vishnu or Krishna, though other communities have other views, and he has a long link with the Varkari tradition of devotional songs by saints such as Dnyaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram. A well-known legend says he came to see his devotee Pundalik, who was serving his parents, and waited on a brick that was thrown out for him to stand on. The name is often read as standing on a brick. The dark stone image stands with its hands on its hips, and each year pilgrims walk from many villages to arrive for Ashadhi Ekadashi. Devotion to him also reaches Karnataka, where Haridasa singers praise Vitthala.
kidSummary: Vithoba is a dear form of God worshipped in a town called Pandharpur. The old story says he waited patiently on a brick for his devotee Pundalik, who was busy caring for his parents. Every year thousands of pilgrims walk and sing for days to visit him.

story.title: A son who cared for his parents
story.text: Pundalik was a devotee who looked after his elderly parents with great love and gave them most of his time.

story.title: A visitor at the door
story.text: In the legend, God came to his door in the form we call Vithoba, but Pundalik was busy serving his parents.

story.title: The brick
story.text: Pundalik tossed out a brick for the visitor to stand on while he waited. God stood patiently on it with his hands on his hips.

story.title: Pundalik finishes his duty
story.text: When he was done, Pundalik came out and was moved to see God still waiting for him.

story.title: He stays
story.text: The story says Vithoba agreed to stay at Pandharpur on the brick, and the place became a great pilgrimage town.

story.title: The walking pilgrims
story.text: Today, Varkari pilgrims walk and sing together to Pandharpur, carrying the palanquins of saints and calling out their love.

teaches: Caring for parents is a form of worship
Everyone can sing and walk together in devotion

facts.text: In Mahipati's telling, a king in Bidar ordered the barber-saint Sena arrested, and Vithoba went to the palace looking like Sena to serve the king, so Sena stayed free to pray.
Vitthala is traditionally read as the one standing on a brick, linking the name to the brick in Pundalik's story.
Saint Tukaram gave a different reading of the name: the one who accepts people, even when they have no learning.
Every year Varkari pilgrims walk to Pandharpur from Alandi and Dehu, the towns of saints Dnyaneshwar and Tukaram, singing devotional songs and carrying the saints' palanquins.
Panduranga means white god, though the image at Pandharpur is dark.
The poet Mahipati tells how Vithoba helped the woman saint Janabai with daily chores such as sweeping the house and pounding rice.
Saint Dnyaneshwar wrote that Vithoba carries Shiva on his head, because Shiva is Vishnu's chief devotee. Some read the cone-shaped crown as a linga.
In some Maharashtrian almanacs and sculptures, Vithoba appears as the ninth avatar of Vishnu in place of the Buddha.
B. R. Ambedkar argued that the Pandharpur image was a depiction of the Buddha, one of several views about the image.
The hereditary priests of the Pandharpur temple say he cannot be pinned down as Vishnu or Shiva: for them, Vithoba is simply Vithoba.

Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara built a Vitthala temple at Hampi, and the Pandharpur image was reportedly taken there for a time; Bhanudas, great-grandfather of the saint Eknath, later brought it back.
A fair is held at Pandharpur on Dussera night, when devotees dance on a large stone slab before the image by torchlight.
The Varkari saints came from many walks of life, including a tailor, a barber, a potter, a Mahar saint and a Muslim saint, Sheikh Muhammad.
About 800,000 Varkaris are reported to travel to Pandharpur for Ashadhi Ekadashi, when the state's chief minister performs a ritual worship.
In Mahipati's account, Damaji, keeper of the royal grain store, shared grain with the people during a famine, and Vithoba came as an outcaste carrying a bag of gold to pay for it.
A tale of the potter-saint Gora Kumbhar says his child was trampled into the clay while he sang Vithoba's name, and Vithoba brought the child back to life.
The Varkari poet-saints mostly address Vithoba as a father, but Janabai, Namdev's maidservant, calls him Vithabai, 'mother Vitthal', in her poems.
Vithoba's consort Rakhumai, whose name means 'mother Rukmini', is also shown with her hands on her hips, standing on a brick, and she has her own separate shrine in the Pandharpur temple complex.
A stone inscription dated 1237 on a beam of the Pandharpur temple records a king donating a village to pay for the food offering to Vitthala, one of the oldest dated records of the god.
The 15th-century saint-poet Kanhopatra, whose abhang songs praise Vithoba, is the only person whose samadhi memorial stands inside the Pandharpur temple precincts. About thirty of her songs survive.
The Pandharpur image is black basalt about 1.14 metres (3 ft 9 in) tall. Its necklace of tulasi beads carries the legendary kaustubha gem, and its earrings are shaped like fish.

The scholar Richard Eaton links the god's arms-on-hips pose to Bir Kuar, a herder's god of the Ahirs of Bihar, and suggests Vithoba was first worshipped as a cowherd Krishna as early as the 6th century.

Namdev, a tailor who lived about 1270 to 1350, praised Vithoba in short Marathi songs called abhangas and sang them in call-and-response kirtan, helping spread a faith that welcomed women and outcastes.
The Dhangar shepherd community sees Vithoba as a brother of their god Viroba, and worships Rakhumai as Padubai, a guardian of cattle.
